paras.text: The study design and analyses were not preregistered. The analyses reported here are entirely new, although they rely on the same dataset as a previously published manuscript (Krenger and Thevenot, 2026). Only two descriptive elements mentioned here were previously reported in the earlier paper: (1) the number of finger users at each testing point, and (2) a descriptive report of the percentages of the different strategies used at each testing point. Importantly, this last information was included only for descriptive purpose and was not accompanied by analyses, interpretation, or discussion. Thus, the present paper is the first to provide an analysis of children's finger strategies. The dataset Krenger and Thevenot (2025) is openly available at:https://osf.io/543yr/overview?view_only=5937fa7b3412495f9849e60c629c1368.

Children frequently count on their fingers to solve addition problems (Butterworth 1999; Krenger and Thevenot 2026; see Neveu et al. 2023 for a review). Regrettably, and despite the fact that several studies indicate that young children who use their fingers to solve additions perform better than those who do not (Dupont‐Boime and Thevenot 2018; Jordan et al. 2008; Krenger and Thevenot 2024; Krenger et al. 2027; Poletti et al. 2025), teachers in kindergarten and primary school still often associate finger counting with math difficulties (Mutlu et al. 2020; Poletti et al. 2023). This negative view of finger counting may stem from the observations that, by the age of 7 or 8, children who do not count on their fingers outperform their peers who do (Jordan et al. 2008). However, recent evidence revealed that efficient non‐finger users at this age are in fact former finger users who have already internalized the strategy (Krenger and Thevenot 2026). This result is compatible with the idea that early finger‐based strategies support the development toward efficient mental strategies (Andres et al. 2008; Fayol and Seron 2005; Krenger and Thevenot 2025; Poletti et al. 2022; Thevenot et al. 2025).

A theoretical account of how the internalization of finger‐based strategies could be supported by finger use itself has been provided by Baroody (1987). This researcher hypothesized a developmental continuity from initial concrete strategies, in which fingers directly represent quantities, to more abstract strategies, in which fingers serve as a mean of keeping track of the addition process to determine a sum (Fuson 1982). More precisely, at the earliest developmental stage, children rely on modeling strategies in which both operands are represented on fingers. The sum is then obtained by counting all raised fingers. For example, to solve 3 + 2, a child might raise three fingers for the first operand and two fingers for the second, then count “1, 2, 3, 4, 5.” This strategy, often referred to as the counting‐all strategy (e.g., Fuson 1982), will be labeled the “modeling” strategy here (Carpenter and Moser 1982). Over time, building on this strategy, children may adopt a more abstract, continuous counting process, in which the two operands are enumerated in a single, uninterrupted sequence. At this stage, children may enumerate the two operands starting from one (i.e., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in our example). This strategy was qualified by Baroody as a modified counting‐all strategy. According to Steffe et al. (1982), before children can implement this continuous single process, they cannot conceive the sum as the extension of one set beyond another prior to initiating a solution. From this intermediate stage, children could gradually shift toward strategies in which they no longer need to represent both operands. Instead, they could initiate counting directly from one of the operands in the problem. The addition 3 + 2 could therefore be solved by starting from “3” and continuing “4, 5,” while raising only two fingers.

Although this gradual transition from concrete to more abstract strategies has been theoretically conceptualized, empirical evidence for this developmental pattern at a large scale is still lacking. Indeed, to date, children's finger‐based strategies have only been observed in small samples (Baroody 1987; Carpenter and Moser 1984; Fuson 1988) and have never been examined longitudinally. The present study aims to address these gaps by documenting the strategies children use from ages 4 ½ to 7 ½ to solve simple additions. Special attention will be given to the description of emerging finger‐based strategies and to the question of whether the development of more advanced strategies is systematically preceded by more basic ones and consistently leads directly to mentalization.

Examining the progression of children from finger modeling strategies to mental strategies is particularly interesting because it reflects children's gradual understanding of the addition concept (Fuson 1982). As illustrated by Siegler's overlapping waves model (1996), children may not transition from one strategy to another in a sudden and definite manner. Even after the emergence of a new strategy based on a better conceptual understanding of addition, this understanding can remain fragile and dependent on the problems’ surface characteristics (Piaget and Inhelder 1964/1941), such as the size of the numbers involved (Ollivier and Lemaire 2024). For example, a child might use a modified counting‐all strategy for 5 + 4, representing the numbers 1 to 9 on fingers and counting them in a single continuous sequence, but be reluctant to use the same strategy for 6 + 3, because one of the operands exceeds the number of fingers on one hand, or for 7 + 4, because it exceeds what can be represented on two hands. This would suggest that the modified counting‐all strategy remains tied to specific situations and that the abstract, general concept on which it depends, namely the extension principle described above (Steffe et al. 1982), has not yet been fully constructed.

To date, only two studies have examined how problem characteristics can influence the type of finger strategies children use. In one study, Dupont‐Boime and Thevenot (2018) reported that six‐year‐old children with higher working memory capacity are more likely to use a counting‐on strategy than their peers with lower capacity, particularly for additions with sums greater than 10. In contrast, children with lower working memory capacities more often rely on modeling strategies, which enables reasonable success for additions up to 10 but led to poorer performance when sums exceeded 10. These findings highlight the importance of both individual differences and problem characteristics in shaping strategy use and performance. However, this study offers limited insight into developmental trajectories, as it does not address how strategies evolve in relation to one another over time. Moreover, the authors’ focus was restricted to modeling and counting‐on strategies, without considering potential transitional strategies (i.e., modified counting all) that may mediate the gradual internalization of addition procedures (Baroody 1987). Finally, the binary distinction between sums below versus above 10 may obscure more subtle ways in which children adapt their strategies to task demands. For instance, as evoked above, additions with sums under 10 can still be challenging to model when one operand exceeds 5 because it prevents children from representing both operands separately on two hands. To capture the interaction between problem characteristics and finger‐based strategies over time, a more fine‐grained approach to the task material is therefore needed.

In the second study addressing the characteristics of problems affecting finger strategies, Bagnoud et al. (2025) used a longitudinal approach in 6‐year‐old children tested twice over a five‐month interval and observed that the developmental trajectories of strategy use diverged between tie, constructed with repeated operands, and non‐tie problems. Specifically, while children tended to shift directly from finger modeling to mental strategies for tie problems, a transitional step involving a counting‐on strategy was more frequently observed for non‐tie problems. While the developmental focus of this study is commendable, this study shares a limitation with Dupont‐Boime and Thevenot (2018) in that the description of strategies was restricted to the representation of one or two operands on fingers, without acknowledging the broader range of strategies children may use. Furthermore, the study did not consider operand size, a factor that can significantly influence children's ability to represent and manipulate quantities using their fingers.

The present study aims to overcome these shortcomings through longitudinal observations of finger‐based strategies, using addition sets carefully designed to elicit a range of different strategies. The three finger strategies described above will be considered, that is the modeling, the counting‐on strategies and the intermediate strategies consisting in representing the two operands in a single and continuous counting process. Instead of using the term “modified counting‐all” proposed by Baroody (1987), we chose to label this strategy “concrete counting‐on.” We did so because, in our view, this terminology better highlights its potential transitional role between a modeling strategy, in which the operands are concretely represented, and a counting‐on strategy, also characterized by a continuous enumeration process.

Concretely, for each addition, it was determined whether children used their fingers or not during the solving process. When fingers were used, it was determined whether a modeling, a concrete counting‐on, a counting‐on or a mental strategy was implemented. For each testing point, the frequency use of each strategy on the whole set(s) of problems presented was calculated. Whether children tended to rely on a single strategy at a given point or used multiple strategies within the same testing point could then be determined. These observations were complemented by considering children's addition skill level. Because the data exploited here have already been used in Krenger and Thevenot (2025) for a different purpose (with no mention of strategies), we already know that children who use their fingers at early developmental stages outperform those who do not. Consequently, we expect that finger users more often pass set 1 than non‐finger users. Over time, all children are expected to pass set 1 and therefore to reach skill level 2. More importantly, among finger‐based strategies, we expect young children to most frequently use the modeling strategy (Baroody 1987; Carpenter and Moser 1982; Dupont‐Boime and Thevenot 2018). Children using this strategy should be able to solve problems in set 1. However, they might be challenged by problems in set 2, in which, as previously noted, one of the operands exceeds 5. Therefore, the key question is whether and when children who rely on the modeling strategy will be able to implement a new finger‐counting strategy to overcome difficulties in set 2. For example, the concrete counting‐on strategy could allow children to solve not only set 1 but also set 2 problems. The counting‐on strategy is expected to emerge later during development (Baroody 1987; Fuson 1982). The next key question is whether, as predicted by Baroody's (1987) model, this counting‐on strategy is frequently preceded by a concrete counting‐on. More generally, the longitudinal design adopted here makes it possible to examine children's developmental trajectories by describing strategy distribution across testing points before the addition process is internalized, or, in other words, before exclusive reliance on mental strategies.

A total of 211 children (108 girls) participated in the study. This sample size was determined by the number of parental consents obtained. Children were recruited from schools located in three relatively small cities in the Vaud Canton, Switzerland. They were predominantly white from middle to relatively high socioeconomic backgrounds. They were first observed at the beginning of their first year of school (prekindergarten; Mage = 4 years, 7 months, SD = 4 months) and tested every six months until the start of their fourth year (Grade 2; Mage = 7 years, 7 months, SD = 4 months). At the first testing point, data from 15 children who did not speak French well enough to understand the tasks were excluded. Their data were included in the analyses once their French proficiency was deemed sufficient. Nonetheless, the entire set of data from one child who was not proficient at T1 and T2 and moved away at T3, and from one child who was not fluent enough until the end of the study, were never considered. In addition, two children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder participated only in a playful manner and their data were also excluded. This resulted in an initial sample of 207 children. However, a few technical issues with video recordings prevented data collection at specific testing points. The precise sample size, along with age and grade at each testing point, is presented in Table 1. It should be noted that most analyses were conducted using all available data, with only the missing observations at the affected testing points removed. The data from an entire child were removed only for the analyses of strategy developmental pathways, which were conducted on the 152 children who participated from the beginning to the end of the study during all sessions. Importantly, Little's (1988) MCAR test yielded a nonsignificant result, χ2 (24) = 31.77, p = 0.130, providing no evidence that the pattern of missingness was systematically related to children's task performance or to other measured characteristics, such as finger use, gender, or age, or to specific additions or sums. Thus, the observed pattern of missing data was compatible with the assumption that data were missing completely at random (MCAR).

Children's behavior during the task was videorecorded to retrospectively analyze the strategies they used to solve the additions and ensure reliable coding. Children's answers and use of fingers were coded using the software BORIS (v. 7.4.11 – 2019–02‐28; Friard and Gamba 2016). Children were considered finger users if, at least once while solving an addition in sets 1 or 2, they visibly moved their fingers sequentially, represented quantities by raising fingers, or physically touched their fingers for counting. In contrast, children who did not exhibit any of these behaviors were classified as non‐finger users.

Chi‐squared tests were used to assess the occurrence of finger use across different testing points. Mixed‐effect binomial models were used to determine the occurrence of strategies across testing points, factoring children's skill levels and/or the set of problems, depending on the specific analysis. To account for repeated measurements on the same children, a random intercept was included in the models. The function glmer of the library lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al. 2017) was used to construct the models. Marginal (R2m: variance explained by the fixed effects only) and conditional R‐squared (R2c: variance explained by both fixed and random effects) were calculated with the MuMIn package (Barton 2023), and the delta method was reported because it provides a more general approximation. In order to test the significance of predictors and their interactions, a Type II Wald chi‐square Analysis of Deviance table was generated with the Anova function of the car package (Fox and Weisberg 2019). Contrasts were calculated with the emmeans package (Lenth 2025). For the sake of concision and simplicity, nonsignificant results are reported only when theoretically relevant. Moreover, only sequential contrasts of interest are reported. However, all other possible pairwise comparisons were performed, but they are reported only when they potentially contradicted the overall result pattern. Contrasts are reported when interactions are significant, except for interactions involving the seven testing points, where only a general description is provided due to the complexity of detailing all contrasts. Finally, to provide a more realistic representation of our results, the percentages reported in the text and tables are based on raw data, calculated by directly averaging over items, rather than on estimated marginal means, which were used in the linear model analyses.

paras.sec_title: Numbers of Children Using each Strategy Combination at Their First and Last Finger‐Use Session
paras.text: Among all children included in this study, 152 were tested from the first to the last testing point. Among them, 10 never used their fingers (see Krenger and Thevenot 2026 for details on these children). For the remaining 142 children, the strategies used at their first observed session of finger use are reported in Table 4. At this first point of finger use, 62 children (43.7%) used a modeling strategy only, 20 (14.1%) used a concrete counting‐on strategy only, and 27 (19.0%) used both strategies. Only 7 (4.9%) used a counting‐on strategy only. To examine how long children continued to rely on their fingers depending on their initial strategy combination, we calculated the mean number of sessions in which finger use was observed1. Children who started with the concrete counting‐on strategy relied on their fingers the longest, averaging 4.6 sessions. In contrast, those who began with the counting‐on strategy used their fingers for an average of 2.1 sessions. Then, we examined which strategies children used immediately before addition was internalized. This was done in the 70 children (out of 142) who had stopped using their fingers before the end of our observations. Just before internalization, 28 of them used a modeling strategy, 14 used a concrete counting‐on strategy, and 31 used a counting‐on strategy. The total number of reported strategies exceeds 70 because some children used more than one strategy before internalization (see Table 4).

In this research, we aimed to describe for the first time the evolution of finger‐based strategies across development. To this end, we adopted a longitudinal design where children aged from 4 ½ to 7 ½ were observed while solving addition problems of increasing difficulty across seven testing points. More precisely, we were interested in determining the successive emergence of the modeling, concrete counting‐on and counting‐on strategies, with the idea that the more concrete strategies could give rise to more abstract ones (Baroody 1987; Fuson 1982).

Our results show that, among finger strategies, the modeling strategy, consisting of representing both addends before combining them to determine the sum, was the most commonly used2 until the age of 6 ½. Moreover, this strategy was also the one that most commonly emerged first during development. Interestingly, this modeling strategy was more often used by young children with the highest arithmetical skill level, who predominantly used this strategy on both Set 1 (71%) and Set 2 problems (47%), where one of the operands exceed the capacity of fingers of one hand. Nonetheless, this attempt was not associated with good performance on Set 2, and it is only from the age of 7 that children begin to shift to the more abstract counting‐on strategy, thereby becoming able to successfully solve less modelizable problems. These observations are consistent with previous accounts in the literature assigning to the modeling strategy a foundational role in the emergence of the counting‐on strategy (Fuson 1982).

This counting‐on strategy was used increasingly over time and became dominant among finger strategies when children were aged 7 ½, that is only at the last point of our observations. At this point, 20% of the problems were still solved using fingers, and almost two‐thirds of them were solved using a counting‐on strategy. This strategy was always associated with very good performance in the addition task, but it must be noted that it was virtually absent in children until the age of 6 ½. In accordance with what was expected, the counting‐on strategy was the dominant strategy right before internalization, and the rare children whom we observed using this strategy at their first session of finger use reached mentalization in fewer sessions than other children. These observations are consistent with previous accounts in the literature considering the counting‐on strategy as reflecting a conception of number on the edge of the possible internalization of the whole calculation process (Fuson 1982). Note, however, that the modeling strategy was also still used by many children just before internalization. This finding is consistent with Bagnoud et al. (2025) conclusion that shifts from counting to mentalization depend on the characteristics of the problems. More specifically, modeling strategies are also frequently used for tie problems immediately before their results can be retrieved from long‐term memory, whereas for non‐tie problems, children tend to internalize the counting procedure directly through counting‐on (see Prado and Thevenot (2026) on the implications of these results within a theoretical developmental account).

If, as just shown, the modeling strategy constitutes the basic approach used by children at the beginning of learning, and the counting‐on strategy represents the last stage before internalization, the question now is whether our data support the existence of a transitional strategy between the two. As explained in the Introduction, the concrete counting‐on strategy has been hypothesized to serve this bridging function, creating a link between the strict modeling of numbers on fingers and a more abstract representation of one of these numbers emerging from a counting‐on process (Baroody 1987). This concrete counting‐on strategy was indeed frequently used by children, with only 51 children out of 142 never observed using it during our observations. Moreover, among the 57 children who used the three strategies during the course of our observations, the most frequent developmental pathway between strategies, observed in 40 children, was the one where the concrete counting‐on strategy emerged between the modeling (or simultaneously with it) and the counting‐on strategies (or simultaneously with it). Finally, compared with the modeling and the counting‐on strategies, the concrete counting‐on strategies was more rarely observed as immediately preceding complete internalization of the addition solving process. All in all, these results support the idea of a transitional role of the concrete counting‐on strategies toward the counting‐on strategy.

Nonetheless, the concrete counting‐on strategy was used more often by children with the lowest addition skills and was associated with poor performance on the addition task, regardless of children's skill level. This may seem surprising for a strategy that is supposed to guide children toward a more advanced level of development. One possible interpretation is that the concrete counting‐on strategy reflects a new conceptual understanding, namely that the quantities involved in an addition do not need to be systematically (re)modeled during the solution process (Steffe et al. 1982) but comes at a performance cost because it places greater demands on working memory than the modeling strategy. Indeed, in the modeling strategy, both operands are externally represented, and solving the problem simply involves counting what is visible. In contrast, during concrete counting‐on, the second operand must be mentally represented while the child simultaneously produces a verbal counting sequence that no longer corresponds to perceptual input. These two conflicting counting tasks, counting the count‐on words, place a substantial load on working memory. It could be only after repetitive failure that children develop a new, more efficient strategy extending their new conceptual understanding that numbers in an addition do not need to be modeled and that the first number provided in a problem corresponds “to the summary of its verbal enumeration [and can thus] be substituted for this enumeration” (p.69, Fuson 1982). The continuous counting process initially used by children in a concrete counting‐on strategy could therefore reach full efficiency only within the counting‐on strategy.

Thus far, we have discussed children who demonstrated all three strategies across our observations. Regarding the 54 children who used only two strategies across testing points, 45 of them followed a pathway consistent with the hypothesis of gradual internalization of the addition process (i.e., modeling before concrete counting‐on; modeling before counting‐on; or concrete counting‐on before counting‐on). Within this group, 20 children who did not transition through the concrete counting‐on strategy, instead shifting directly from modeling to counting‐on before mentalization, are also considered to conform to the hypothesized pathway. Indeed, according to Fuson (1982), children transition can spontaneously shift from one strategy to another when they realize that, in the modeling strategy, they unnecessarily recount the same objects or repeat the same words.

Until now, we have described the trajectories that children most often follow toward mentalization, which are congruent with our hypothesis. However, it should be noted that 26 of the 142 children who displayed at least two strategies did not follow this pattern. For example, within children who used only two strategies, 7 used the concrete counting‐on strategy before the modeling strategy, and 2 used counting‐on before modeling. Moreover, 31 children were observed using only one strategy before reaching mentalization, which does not conform either with the idea of a gradual internalization of strategies. Despite further investigation using external measures of arithmetical abilities, we found no evidence that these children exhibited lower skills than those who more closely followed the hypothesized pathways toward internalization3. Then, although we identified a dominant developmental pattern in the emergence of finger strategies, it is important to keep in mind that several different behavioral profiles can be observed, and, that, as in many areas of development, children's progress cannot be reduced to a single, uniform pathway. Moreover, even among children described here as following the hypothesized pathway toward mentalization, numerous shifts back and forth between strategies across sessions (see Appendix A) confirm that cognitive development does not always follow a monotonic progression toward a final state (Siegler 1996).

Still, as demonstrated in the present research, there is an order in the succession of finger strategies that children preferentially adopt before solving addition problems mentally. Modeling strategies are most often observed before concrete counting‐on or counting‐on strategies and the concrete counting‐on strategy is typically observed before counting‐on. Nevertheless, at this stage of our investigation, and despite the fact that this sequence order is not arbitrary and is theoretically justified, it is not possible to assert that one strategy directly stems from the preceding one. Such a conclusion could only be drawn from intervention studies in which one strategy is explicitly taught with the expectation that it will accelerate the emergence of the subsequent strategy. One attempt in this direction was made by Baroody (1987), who trained 17 children in the modeling strategy and observed the effect on the emergence of more advanced strategies. The results were inconclusive, but, as acknowledged by the author, this may have been due to the small sample size. Future studies with larger samples are needed to test whether mastery of one strategy facilitates the acquisition of the next in the developmental sequence. More generally, regarding the teaching of specific finger‐counting strategies, it is possible that, for at least some of the children we observed, these strategies were not self‐discovered, as we have implicitly assumed throughout this discussion, but were explicitly taught by teachers or parents at home. In this context, counting‐on is the strategy most likely to have been explicitly taught, because it is generally considered the most efficient strategy by educators and is sometimes recommended for practice (e.g., Education Endowment Foundation [EEF], 2023). Future studies should therefore investigate the extent to which children's use of counting‐on or other strategies at a given point in development stems from their use of previous strategies or occurs independently as a result of explicit teaching.

Before concluding, there are two points to consider when reflecting on our results. First, it is possible that some critical observations had been missed during the course of the study. Indeed, because testing sessions were spaced six months apart, it is possible that some strategies were adopted and subsequently abandoned between two assessment points without being observed. More frequent testing, every three months or even monthly, might have reduced this issue, but the possibility of missing observations can never be entirely ruled out. Moreover, the fact that a dominant pattern of behaviors emerged across testing points indicates that, at the very least, our design was sufficiently fine‐grained to capture a meaningful developmental trajectory of children's finger strategy use prior to mental addition. Second, we reported that children in our sample came from middle to higher socioeconomical backgrounds and the transferability of our conclusion to children from lower backgrounds will be necessary in the future. In fact, even at the scale of this study, the robustness of our conclusions is interesting to investigate across schools. A complementary analysis of our results revealed that there was no overall effect of finger use across schools (χ2(2, N = 1253) = 1.539, p = 0.453). However, at the final testing point of our study, children from the city with the lowest socioeconomic status among the three cities in which we conducted our investigation showed more frequent finger use than children from the other two cities (χ2(2, N = 165) = 5.827, p = 0.054). This is consistent with the pattern observed by Jordan et al. (2008), who found that children from lower‐SES backgrounds rely on finger counting for a longer period than children from higher‐SES backgrounds. Nonetheless, such subtle differential patterns in our results encourage further research in diverse cultural contexts, including across different countries, to extend and further assess the generalizability of our conclusions.
